text: One swing of the ladle, and the crawler bursts into ash. The ladle rings like a bell.
Geum's slippers haven't moved an inch. Steam curls off her steel arm.
Jaeha just stares up at her, bleeding, while the old fisherman crawls away.
Two more crawlers come out of the water. She smashes one with her steel arm and stamps on the other.
But Jaeha is watching the ladle. A faint ring of force spreads off it.
That wasn't a hard hit, Auntie. No, she says, wiping the ladle on her apron. It was a held one.
The sea's been getting bolder since Sunday. Jaeha asks about the man ten years ago, and this time she says, sit down. This one's a long set.
So they sit on the parapet, his arm wrapped in his towel, Nib keeping watch.
Ten years ago. The night the gates opened.
The sea off Busan boiled violet. Boats burned. And at the neck of the breakwater, a line of fishermen held behind one short, broad woman.
Geum was fifty-two, and she sold fish. That night she woke up strong, tore a steel door off a boat, and held the line with it.
Then a young man walked past her, the wrong way. Ahead of him walked fighters made of light, and in the water swam something enormous, carrying a lantern.
He sent them all in first.
Geum remembers thinking, who sends people in first like that?
Then he knelt on the concrete, a few steps past her line, and bled for them. Nose, hands. Just like Jaeha does.
And then he stopped bleeding.
Because he'd stopped carrying them. Their lights went out under the water, one by one, the great lantern last. Not one came back.
He walked out to the end of the breakwater and into the sea, toward the violet light, and was gone. She never saw his face.
Then something rose out of the sea, too big to see the end of, with the same lantern on its head, burning violet.
A hand the size of a building came down on her. She held it. Her arm didn't.
It sank at dawn. For three days, all of Busan built a lid over the gate out of its own stones. It's been pushing ever since.
Back in the present, she looks at her steel hand. I've stood on this breakwater every night since.
Someone carried like him. And then he stopped.
Jaeha looks at his shaking hands. He stopped carrying, and they died. That's what she saw, Geum says. What it means, she doesn't know.
She taps his chest with the ladle. So you'll get a body that never has to stop.
Wednesday morning, a market auntie comes running. Something's glowing in the cold store.
Between the racks of frozen fish hangs a brand-new gate. Grade D. Unregistered.
The sea is leaking, Geum says. Little gates pop up when the big one cracks. Call the Association? She's retired, not dead.
Today's rule: no carrying. Not one drop. Then who takes their hits? They do. They're soldiers, not eggs.
Jaeha hesitates, then switches off his own skill for one gate.
Nib goes through first, as always.
Inside is a flooded Far Side shrine, knee-deep in sea water, with something sitting on the altar.
Nib, Borro and Lyra flare into field form. Linked, but not carried.
It stands up: a hermit crab four metres tall, wearing a stone shrine as its shell, a bronze bell clanging inside.
Its big claw slams Borro into a pillar and pins him there.
Every instinct screams at Jaeha to take the hit. Geum's steel hand clamps his shoulder. No.
Lyra's arrows bounce off the stone shell, and she is not happy about it.
Nib slashes a leg, and the smaller claw flings him into a pillar, cutting his arm open.
He gets up bleeding and glares back. Don't you dare carry this.
Jaeha shakes. They chose to go first, kid. Let them. If someone's dying, she'll step in. Nobody's dying.
Then Jaeha notices the crab keeps tapping Borro's shell, while its own cramped shrine crumbles.
Hermit crabs trade up. It wants Borro's shell.
So Borro gets the strangest order of his career. Look roomy. Roomy?
Borro does his best to look like an empty house.
It works. The Hermit hauls its soft body out to move in, and for two seconds it's bare.
Jaeha barely moves his lips. Lyra. Now.
Her arrow goes straight through it, and Nib drives both knives into the crack in its shell.
The Hermit bursts into ash, and its empty shrine topples, the bell rolling into the water.
Borro pats his shell shut, deeply offended. He is not roomy.
Boss defeated. A new kind, so Route Alignment hits a hundred percent.
Then a level-up: Operator level seven, a fourth summon slot, six minutes of field form.
And once again, the only option is harvest. Jaeha is still writing that down.
Nib holds his cut arm. You didn't carry me. You said don't you dare. Good.
Geum grins, gold tooth flashing. That's how a wall stays up. You let it do its job.
She pays everyone in fish cakes, and Lyra notices Borro got one more.
That night, Jaeha stands where the man stood ten years ago, with a call waiting.
Geum comes to stand beside him. Call them, then. Whoever's out there.
He touches the mark.
Black water under a starless sky. One rift is lit: a broken signal tower, and something fluffy on top.
Then two enormous black eyes appear an inch from his face. Finally! I've been waiting forever!
